morningLine: IBM comes home, Apple gets arcade muscle, and Activision moves two cartridge hits onto Atari computers.

lead.headline: IBM Cracks Open 'Peanut' and Sends PCjr Into the Home
lead.dek: The world's largest computer maker formally entered the home-computer contest on November 1, aiming above low-cost rivals while extending IBM PC software compatibility.
body: NEW YORK—After months of speculation about a machine code-named “Peanut,” International Business Machines formally unveiled the PCjr on November 1. The announcement puts the company that defined the business-PC standard directly into the crowded home-computer market, with deliveries planned for early 1984.

IBM priced a 64K system unit with a battery-powered cordless infrared keyboard at $669. A $1,269 package raises memory to 128K and adds a diskette drive. Neither price includes a monitor or printer; IBM's color display is $680, while a compact printer is $175.

The unusual keyboard can work from as far as 20 feet away. IBM cautioned that several PCjrs operating in one room would need cords to avoid infrared interference, a curious limitation for classrooms—one of the markets the company says it is pursuing alongside homes and small businesses.

Software compatibility may be the machine's strongest calling card. IBM said most programs written for the IBM PC should run on PCjr unless they demand more memory, while cartridge support and television compatibility aim to make the junior machine friendlier in the living room.

The PCjr arrives above the bargain end of the market and accessories quickly lift the full-system cost. Still, IBM's entry changes the stakes: home computing now has the attention of the industry's largest name, and every rival will have to answer it.

stories.headline: Apple II Gets an Arcade Board
stories.dek: A $225 expansion board promised coin-op-style graphics and sound while giving BASIC programmers more than 40 new commands.
body: Third Millennium Engineering introduced the Arcade Board for the Apple II, II Plus, and IIe. The board used many of the same video and sound chips found in coin-operated games.

It shipped with more than 20 demos, games, and utilities and extended Applesoft BASIC with more than 40 commands. The advertised price was $225. A $225 expansion board promised coin-op-style graphics and sound while giving BASIC programmers more than 40 new commands.

stories.headline: Activision Moves River Raid and Kaboom! to Atari Computers
stories.dek: Two best-selling cartridge games crossed from console to Atari home computers, illustrating publishers' push toward the computer-game market during the console downturn.
body: COMPUTE!'s November 1983 product pages reported Atari-computer conversions of Activision's River Raid and Kaboom!. The conversions were enhanced to use the greater capabilities of Atari home computers.

The news followed Atari's late-October move to publish games for competitors' machines, evidence of rapidly shifting platform economics. Two best-selling cartridge games crossed from console to Atari home computers, illustrating publishers' push toward the computer-game market during the console downturn.

stories.headline: Touch-Sensitive PowerPad Offers a New Way to Control Home Computers
stories.dek: Chalk Board's 12-inch touch surface represented an early consumer alternative to keyboard input.
body: The Chalk Board PowerPad was described as a touch-sensitive input device replacing the keyboard for supported tasks. Its active surface measured 12 by 12 inches.
COMPUTE! carried the product in its November 1983 news pages. Chalk Board's 12-inch touch surface represented an early consumer alternative to keyboard input.
